entries.modern_form: PIE *(s)ker- 'to turn, bend' (Pokorny's 3. (s)ker-, IEW 935-938; Watkins/AHD sker-3)
entries.note: Root, language label, gloss and page are all right. Pokorny IEW 935-938 heads the lemma '(s)ker-3', Meaning: 'to turn, bend', with the note '(see also 1. (s)ker- "shrivel, shrink" and 2. (s)ker- "spring")'; Walde-Pokorny II 568 ff. print it as '(s)qer- "drehen, biegen"'; Watkins closes his sker-3 entry '[Pok. 3. (s)ker- 935.]'. Nourai's numbering 'Sker 1 / Sker 2' is his own and does not match Pokorny's (Nourai's Sker 2 is a redirect to Sek). Two cautions that colour the whole page: (i) Watkins himself calls this the 'presumed base of a number of distantly related derivatives' — it is a bundle of guttural, dental and labial extensions rather than one tight family, and Nourai's two intermediate boxes (*Kor-ōna, *Kur-wo) are made to carry children that in his own sources hang from quite different extensions; (ii) the Iranian branch (Av. karana- 'end, edge' > Pahl. kanār > NP karān/kanār) is attached to this root on Mann's authority alone — Buck, at the page Nourai cites, writes 'etym.?', and Pokorny/Walde-Pokorny list under this root only Avestan skarəna- 'round', not karana-.
entries.note_fa: ریشه، برچسب زبانی، معنا و شمارهٔ صفحه همگی درست‌اند: پوکورنی در صفحات ۹۳۵ تا ۹۳۸ سرواژهٔ «(s)ker-3» را با معنای «پیچیدن، خمیدن» آورده و یادآور شده که آن را با «(s)ker- ۱ (چروکیدن)» و «(s)ker- ۲ (جهیدن)» اشتباه نگیرند؛ والده-پوکورنی (ج ۲ ص ۵۶۸ به بعد) همان را با املای «(s)qer- «drehen, biegen»» ثبت کرده‌اند و واتکینز نیز مدخل sker-3 خود را با «[پوکورنی ۳. (s)ker- ص ۹۳۵]» به پایان می‌برد. شماره‌گذاری «Sker 1 / Sker 2» از آنِ خود نورایی است و با شماره‌گذاری پوکورنی نمی‌خواند. دو هشدار که بر کل این صفحه سایه می‌افکند: نخست آنکه خود واتکینز این را «پایهٔ مفروض شماری مشتقات دورخویشاوند» می‌خواند، یعنی مجموعه‌ای از گسترش‌های گوناگون است نه یک خانوادهٔ فشرده؛ و نورایی دو جعبهٔ میانی خود (*Kor-ōna و *Kur-wo) را وادار کرده فرزندانی را بپذیرند که در مأخذ خودِ او از گسترش‌های دیگری می‌آیند. دوم آنکه شاخهٔ ایرانی (اوستایی karana- «کرانه» ← پهلوی kanār ← فارسی کران/کنار) تنها بر پایهٔ مان به این ریشه بسته شده است؛ باک در همان صفحه‌ای که نورایی ارجاع می‌دهد می‌نویسد «ریشه‌شناسی؟» و پوکورنی و والده-پوکورنی زیر این ریشه تنها skarəna- اوستایی «گرد» را می‌آورند نه karana- را.

Avestan skarana- "round" ... gr. κυρτός "crooked" ... κορωνός ... Latin curvus ... References: WP. II 568 ff., WH. I 220 f. ... Page(s): 935-938'. The page number is exact and the gloss is verbatim.

consulted.note: '(s)q[er- "drehe]n, biegen" (s. auch sqer- "einschrumpfen" und sqer- "springen"). ... Av. skarəna- "rund" ... gr. κυρτός "krumm" ... κορωνός "gekrümmt" ... lat. curvus "krumm, gekrümmt, gewölbt" (Formans -no- oder allenfalls von der eu-Basis)'.

'sker-3. Also ker-. To turn, bend. Presumed base of a number of distantly related derivatives. ... [Pok. 3. (s)ker- 935.]' — the whole of Nourai's page 424 is an expansion of this single appendix entry plus the Iranian branch.

Mann does not have one root but four adjacent lemmas: 'kor- "bend, curve; bent, curved"' (p.533), 'korōn-, korən- "edge, rim, border"' (p.535), 'korono- "curve-"' (p.536) and '(kuruos "bent, round". Assumed for Latin only)'. Nourai's two intermediate boxes conflate them.
'Av. karana- (also in special senses "border, shore", etc.; NPers. karan "shore, side"), etym.? Barth. 451.' — Buck supplies the Iranian words but declines to assign them a root.

nodes.derivation: The starred *kor-ōna of the chart is Watkins's 'Suffixed o-grade form *kor-ó-no- in Greek korōnos, curved' (AHD appendix s.v. sker-3, §10) and Pokorny's 'κορωνός "gekrümmt"; κορώνη "allerlei Gekrümmtes, Gebogenes etc." (Latin loanword corona), perhaps as *kor[u]-no-s to the u-basis *(s)kereu-' (IEW 935). An o-grade *kor- of *(s)ker- enlarged with -no-/-ōno- is therefore genuine, and the gloss 'bent' fits the Greek adjective. Two reservations: (a) the shape written 'Kor-ôna' with final -a reproduces the Greek feminine κορώνη rather than a neutral IE stem; (b) the second reference Nourai gives, Mann IEC 535, is not a lemma meaning 'bent' at all — p. 535 has 'korōn-, korən- "edge, rim, border". Cf. kor- and WP I, 413, II, 591 — Per. karán, id.; Gk. korṓnē, id. (and "curve, crown". LW in Lat. corona)', while Mann's 'curve' lemmas stand on pp. 533 (kor- 'bend, curve') and 536 (korono- 'curve-'). Nourai has fused Mann's 'edge' root (which is what the Iranian branch below needs) with Pokorny's 'curved' root into a single box.
nodes.derivation_fa: صورت بازسازی‌شدهٔ *kor-ōna در این نمودار همان چیزی است که واتکینز در پیوست ریشه‌های هندواروپایی فرهنگ AHD زیر sker-3 آورده است: «صورت پسوندی درجهٔ o یعنی *kor-ó-no- در یونانی korōnós «خمیده»»؛ پوکورنی نیز در ص ۹۳۵ همین را با κορωνός «خمیده» و κορώνη «هر چیز خمیده و کمانی» (که وام‌واژهٔ لاتینی corona از آن است) ثبت کرده. پس ستاک درجهٔ o از ریشهٔ *(s)ker- با پسوند -no-/-ōno- واقعی است و معنای «خمیده» درست. اما دو نکته: نخست آنکه املای Kor-ôna با -a پایانی در واقع صورت مؤنث یونانی κορώνη است نه ستاک هندواروپایی؛ دوم آنکه مأخذ دوم نورایی، مان (IEC) ص ۵۳۵، اصلاً سرواژه‌ای به معنای «خمیده» ندارد بلکه *korōn-/korən- «کناره، لبه، مرز» است و همان‌جا «فارسی karān» را می‌آورد. نورایی دو ریشهٔ جدا (یکی «خمیده» و یکی «کناره») را در یک جعبه درآمیخته است؛ بنابراین ادعا با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: Avestan karana- is real and exactly as glossed: Bartholomae, AiW col. 451, 'j. karana- m. "Ende"; 1) räumlich: "Grenze, Rand; Ufer; Flügel (des Heeres)"' (uva karana aŋhå zəmō Yt.10.95 'both ends of this earth'; upa yaozəṇta karana zrayå vouru.kaṣ̌aya Yt.5.38 'on the surging shores [of Lake Vourukaṣ̌a]'), the temporal sense 'end' only in compounds; Bartholomae's KompE. note already adds 'np. kanār, kanāra'. Two problems with the chart. (a) The label 'Old Persian' is unsupported: Kent's Old Persian lexicon has no karana- (a grep of KNT.txt returns nothing); the word is Avestan (with Middle and New Iranian continuants), and Nourai's own two references, Bartholomae and Buck, are both Avestan. (b) The arrow from *kor-ōna 'bent' is not established. Buck, the very page cited, writes 'Av. karana- (also in special senses "border, shore", etc.; NPers. karan "shore, side"), etym.?' (SYN 857) — i.e. he declines to give it a root. Walde-Pokorny and Pokorny list under (s)ker- 'turn, bend' only Avestan skarəna- 'round', never karana-. Modern Wiktionary derives Proto-Iranian *karana- 'edge, border, limit' from a root *kar- 'to draw a line, furrow' or *kar- 'to cut' (i.e. Pokorny's (s)ker-4 'cut', p. 938), with *(s)ker- 'bend' only one of the possibilities.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian kanār [kn'l] 'side, edge; embrace' and its -ag derivative kanārag [kn'lk'] 'edge, limit, boundary' are both in MacKenzie's Concise Pahlavi Dictionary (p. 49-50), with Manichaean MP kn'rg and the privative a-kanārag 'unlimited, boundless'; Nyberg's glossary has 'kanārak [kn'lk'; ŠTL'] boundary ... MPrs kn'rg "side"; Paz. kanāra; NP kanārah "side, shore"'. The -n- where Avestan karana- has -r- is Hübschmann's 'Umstellung von Konsonanten verschiedener Silben' (Persische Studien p. 267), the same dissimilatory transposition as hargiz beside older hagirz and bižišk/hižišk: karana- > *kanār beside the regularly inherited karān, with loss of the final vowel and lengthening in the open second syllable giving MP -ār. Horn, Grundriss p. 189, states the chain exactly as the chart draws it: 'aw. karana- "Seite, Ende"; phlv. kanār, kanārak'. Moʿin's footnote in Borhān-e Qāṭeʿ p. 1699 s.v. کنار cites Darmesteter to the same effect.
nodes.derivation_fa: فارسی میانه (پهلوی) kanār «سو، کناره؛ آغوش» و مشتق آن kanārag «لبه، مرز، حد» هر دو در فرهنگ مکنزی (ص ۴۹–۵۰) ثبت‌اند، همراه با صورت پارتی/مانوی kn'rg و صورت منفی a-kanārag «بی‌کران»؛ نیبرگ نیز kanārak را با معنی «مرز» آورده و آن را با «kanāra پازند» و «کنارهٔ فارسی نو» می‌سنجد. تبدیل r… r به n… r در این واژه همان چیزی است که هوبشمان آن را «جابه‌جایی همخوان‌های دو هجا» (قلب) می‌نامد (پژوهش‌های فارسی، ص ۲۶۷) و آن را در کنار hargiz/hagirz و بزشک/هزشک می‌گذارد: از اوستایی karana- هم karān (بی‌قلب) و هم kanār (با قلب) به دست آمده است. هرن در ص ۱۸۹ همین زنجیره را می‌آورد و معین نیز در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع ص ۱۶۹۹ به نقل از دارمستتر همین را می‌گوید. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: All four Persian words are real and current: کران karān 'edge, border, limit', کرانه karāna 'shore, margin', کنار kanār 'side, shore; embrace', کناره kanāra 'edge, shore'. But the chart's chain Pahlavi kanār -> Persian karān is inverted for karān itself. New Persian karān continues Middle Persian karan [kl'n'] 'side, edge, end, limit' (MacKenzie 1971: 49), the regular, untransposed descendant of Avestan karana- (final -a lost, the stressed second syllable lengthened to -ān); کنار/کناره are the doublets that came down through the transposed MP kanār(ag). Wiktionary s.v. کران says just that — 'from Middle Persian klʾn' /karān/, from Proto-Iranian *karana-' — and files کنار as 'a metathesized form' of it; Wiktionary s.v. کنار likewise: 'from Middle Persian knʾl /kanār/ ... a metathesis of کران (karân)'. Horn p. 189 lists the whole set side by side without making either the parent of the other. So karān and kanār are siblings, not parent and child; کرانه and کناره are the -a extensions of each.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر چهار صورت «کران، کرانه، کنار، کناره» واژه‌های اصیل فارسی‌اند، اما زنجیرهٔ نمودار (پهلوی kanār ← فارسی کران) وارونه است. «کران» دنبالهٔ فارسی میانهٔ karan «سو، لبه، پایان، حد» (مکنزی ص ۴۹) است که خود بازماندهٔ بی‌قلبِ اوستایی karana- است: واکهٔ پایانی افتاده و هجای دوم کشیده شده (karana- > karān). در برابر، «کنار» و «کناره» از صورت مقلوبِ پهلوی kanār/kanārag آمده‌اند. ویکی‌واژه ذیل «کران» می‌نویسد: «از فارسی میانهٔ karān، از ایرانی آغازین *karana-» و «کنار» را «صورت مقلوب کران» می‌خواند. هرن نیز در ص ۱۸۹ هر دو دسته را در کنار هم و هم‌ردیف می‌آورد. پس «کران» فرزند «کنار» نیست بلکه خواهر آن است؛ ادعای نورایی با این تصحیح پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: Avestan a-karana- adj. (fem. -nā-) 'endlos' is Bartholomae AiW col. 46 (BRT.txt leaf 62), a bahuvrihi of the privative prefix a- (PIE *n̥-, the chart's cross-reference 'Ne 1') with karana- 'end'. It is the standing epithet of boundless time and boundless light in the Younger Avesta: zrvan- akarana- 'Unbegrenzte Zeit' (V.19.9, AiW quoting 'in der unbegrenzten Zeit'), and akarana anaγra asaonō stiš (Yt.13.48) 'the endless, beginningless creation of the Righteous One'. The compound is continued unbroken into Middle Persian a-kanārag 'unlimited, boundless' (MacKenzie p.50) and akanārakēh 'boundlessness ... of Ohrmazd' (Nyberg), and into New Persian بی‌کران. As for Old Persian, the word is not attested there either (see node #2).

nodes.derivation: The transmission itself is textbook: Latin corōna 'garland, wreath, crown' is an early borrowing of Greek κορώνη, which Klein states plainly ('corona, n., a crown. — L. corona, "garland, wreath, crown", fr. Gk. κορώνη, "anything curved; a wreath, garland"'); from Latin came Old French corone/curune, Anglo-Norman corune, Middle English coroune, whence crown (in English from c.1200, with the Norman monarchy, and applied to the coin from 1526); corona was re-borrowed straight from Latin as a learned term (architectural member, 16th c.; the halo of the sun, 1809). Two qualifications keep this from 'confirmed'. (a) The immediate Greek source is the feminine noun κορώνη, not the adjective κορωνός drawn as its parent — they are related but distinct words. (b) The deeper tie to *(s)ker- is now contested: Beekes, followed by Wiktionary, derives κορώνη from PIE *ḱorh₂- 'crow, raven' (whence Latin cornix), the 'curved object' senses arising secondarily from the crow's beak; on that view crown/corona drop out of this root altogether. Watkins still lists CORONA, CROWN under sker-3.

nodes.derivation: *kur-wo- is Watkins's reconstruction, taken over verbatim: 'sker-3 ... 4. Suffixed variant form *kur-wo- in Latin curvus, bent, curved: CURB, CURVATURE, CURVE, CURVET.' Pokorny (935) gives only the Latin word with the parenthesis '(forms -uo-)', and Mann is blunter still: '(kuruos "bent, round". Assumed for Latin only, cf. kor-)'. So a zero-grade *kur- with a -wo- suffix is a legitimate inference for curvus (and, without the suffix, for Greek kyrtós, Ernout-Meillet s.v. curuus 'Même vocalisme que dans gr. κυρτός'), but it is a Latin-internal reconstruction, not an inherited IE stem with a wide progeny. The chart nevertheless hangs on it Old Persian Kūru-, Greek krikos, Latin crista/crispus and the whole Germanic group — none of which come from *kur-wo- in any of Nourai's own sources: Watkins derives them from *ki-kr-o- (krikos), *kris-tā- (crista), *krip-so- (crispus), *(s)kre-n-g- (shrink), *(s)kre-n-gh- (*hringaz) and *kreuk- (*hrugjaz). The added gloss 'curly' is imported from crispus. Read as a cover label for the *kur-/*kr- side of the root the box is harmless; read as a node it overstates.

nodes.derivation: The FORMS are exactly right and are lifted, with the KNT:180 reference, from Moʿin: the Old Persian stem is Kūru-, nominative singular Kūruš (CMa 1 adam Kūruš xšāyaθiya 'I am Cyrus the King'), genitive singular Kūrauš (DB 1.28 Kabūjiya nāma Kūrauš puça 'Cambyses by name, a son of Cyrus'), beside Elamite Ku-raš and Babylonian Ku-ra-aš — Kent, Old Persian p. 180: 'Kūru- sb. "Cyrus", founder of the Persian Empire: Elam. ku-raš, Akk. ku-ra-aš, Gk. Κῦρος (§164.V).' (Nourai's '559 BC' is the traditional date of Cyrus II's accession in Anšan, not his birth.) The MEANING is where the node fails. Kent files the name under §164.V 'Uncertain names: Čišpi-; Kūru-; Dātuvahya-; Arxa-', i.e. he expressly gives it no etymology; and no standard authority reads it as 'curly hair'. Rüdiger Schmitt (Enc. Iranica, 'Cyrus i. The Name') says the etymology 'remains in dispute' and prefers Karl Hoffmann's *kuru- 'humiliator of the enemy in verbal contest' (to a root *(s)kau-); J. Harmatta took it to an Iranian kur- 'be born', hence 'young one'; J. Tavernier regards Elamite Kuraš as primary, 'to bestow care'; Wiktionary adds a possible Urartian toponym Quriani (the upper Kura). 'Curly hair' from *kur-wo- is a modern popular etymology built on Latin curvus/crispus and rests only on FAF:513, which is not accessible.

nodes.derivation: The Persian name کوروش Kuruš/Kūroš is not an unbroken inheritance: the Achaemenid name left no trace in Middle or Classical New Persian (Ferdowsi's Šāhnāma has no Cyrus), and the modern form is a nineteenth/twentieth-century restoration read off the cuneiform after Rawlinson's decipherment — which is exactly why Moʿin's entry is a transliteration exercise citing Kent rather than a lexical article. کورش beside کوروش is merely the spelling with and without the waw for OP -u-. The gloss '"sun"' is not modern scholarship but Ctesias': Plutarch, Artaxerxes 1.3, reports 'Cyrus' as named after 'the sun, which in the Persian language is called Cyrus' (an association with Old Iranian hvar / New Persian خور 'sun'). Nourai takes it from Funk & Wagnalls, which prints '[Per., the sun.]' at the end of its Cyrus entry. Modern scholars reject it outright (see node #9); the phonetics do not work, since hvar- gives NP xor/xvar, not kur-. So the arrow OP Kūru- > NP کوروش is right in substance but modern and learned, and the gloss is a classical folk etymology.

nodes.derivation: Greek Κῦρος is the regular Hellenisation of Old Persian Kūruš: the Persian nominative ending -š is dropped and replaced by the Greek masculine o-stem ending -ος, the long ū being written υ. It is in use from the first half of the fifth century BCE — Aeschylus, Persians 768, and throughout Herodotus I — i.e. contemporary with the Achaemenids, so a direct oral borrowing, not a literary one; the later itacistic variant Κόρος also occurs. Kent lists 'Gk. Κῦρος' among the reflexes of Kūru- at the page Nourai cites for the parent node, and Moʿin's entry repeats it. Funk & Wagnalls, Nourai's reference here, gives the name and its Romance/Germanic equivalents (F. Cyrus, G. Cyrus, It. Ciro, Sp. Ciro); only its bracketed gloss '[Per., the sun.]' is obsolete.

nodes.derivation: An empty-word node: the book gives only the two Persian spellings. Both are re-borrowings of the Western form of the name back into Persian, so the arrow Greek > Persian is right in substance but the route is modern and European, not an ancient Greek loan into Persian. کوروس Kūrūs simply transliterates Greek Κῦρος / Latin Cyrus. سیروس Sīrus renders the FRENCH pronunciation of Cyrus, [siʁys], and entered Persian as a given name in the late Qajar / early Pahlavi period, alongside the restored کوروش; Persian Wikipedia s.v. سیروس says «سیروس یونانی‌شدهٔ نام فارسی کوروش است» ('Sirus is the Hellenised form of the Persian name Kuruš'). The pair کوروش ~ سیروس is thus a doublet of exactly the same kind as پارس ~ فارس or مهرداد ~ Mithridates: the native form and its Europeanised return.

nodes.derivation: English Cyrus comes through Latin Cȳrus (Cicero, De divinatione; the Vulgate of Isaiah 44-45, Ezra 1, Daniel 1) from Greek Κῦρος, with the regular Latin transcription of υ as y and of the Greek -ος as -us. It is not a learned modern borrowing from the cuneiform but a Bible name: the Wycliffite and then the Geneva and King James versions carry it, and it became a common English (especially Puritan and later American) given name from the seventeenth century, whence Cyrus McCormick, Cyrus Field and the like. Funk & Wagnalls p. 644 has exactly this entry ('Cyrus ... 1. A masculine personal name ... 2. "The Great" ... king of Persia: founder of the Persian empire'); only its closing gloss '[Per., the sun.]' is the obsolete Ctesian etymology discussed at node #10. The chain drawn — Old Persian > Greek > English — is right, with Latin as the unnamed intermediate.
nodes.derivation_fa: صورت انگلیسی Cyrus از راه Cȳrus لاتین (سیسرون؛ ترجمهٔ ولگات در اشعیا ۴۴–۴۵، عزرا ۱ و دانیال ۱) از Κῦρος یونانی آمده است، با تبدیل قاعده‌مند υ یونانی به y و پایانهٔ -ος به -us در لاتین. این نام وام‌گیری نوِ عالمانه از کتیبه‌های میخی نیست بلکه نامی کتاب‌مقدسی است: از ترجمهٔ ویکلیف و سپس ترجمه‌های ژنو و شاه جیمز به انگلیسی رسید و از سدهٔ هفدهم به بعد (به‌ویژه نزد پیوریتن‌ها و سپس در آمریکا) نام کوچک رایجی شد. فرهنگ فانک و واگنالز در ص ۶۴۴ همین مدخل را دارد؛ تنها یادداشت پایانی آن «[فارسی: خورشید]» ریشه‌شناسی منسوخ کتزیاسی است که در گرهٔ ۱۰ بحث شد. زنجیرهٔ نمودار (پارسی باستان ← یونانی ← انگلیسی) درست است و تنها حلقهٔ لاتین در آن نامبرده نشده است.

nodes.words: curve, curb, curvature; crest; crisp, crepe
nodes.derivation: Watkins lists exactly this set under sker-3: '§4 ... Latin curvus ...: CURB, CURVATURE, CURVE, CURVET'; '§6 ... Latin crista ...: CREST, CRISTA, CRISTATE'; '§7 ... Latin crispus ...: CREPE, CRISP, CRISPATE'. Routes: curve is Latin curvāre taken into English as a verb in the fifteenth century (the noun 1690s); curb is Old French courber 'to bend' < curvāre, into Middle English as a horse's chin-strap, then 'restrain', then the stone edging of a pavement; curvature is Latin curvātūra, sixteenth century. crest is Middle English creste < Old French creste (modern crête) < Latin crista (Klein s.v. crest). crisp is the oldest of them: it was borrowed straight into Old English from Latin crispus and meant 'curly' for a thousand years before the modern 'brittle' sense took over (Klein: 'crisp, adj. — OE., fr. L. crispus "curly"'); crepe is French crêpe, feminine of crêp(e) < Latin crispus, 'crinkled silk gauze', borrowed in the eighteenth century, so crisp and crepe are doublets.

nodes.derivation: Latin circus 'ring, circular line; the (round) racecourse' is at IEW 936 in the same paragraph as Greek κίρκος/κρίκος. The arrow Greek > Latin is a borrowing, and that is how the standard handbooks take it: Klein, 'L. circus, "a circle, ring, a round enclosure for games", more prob. borrowed from, than cogn. with Gk. κίρκος, κρίκος, "a ring"' — the loan will have come with the Greek hippodrome vocabulary of Magna Graecia in the third century BCE. Ernout-Meillet note that the original sense was simply 'cercle', which was then taken over by the diminutive circulus, leaving circus attached to the building ('sens premier "cercle", mais a été remplacé dans cette acception par le diminutif circulus, et a tendu à ne plus désigner que le "cirque"'). So the chart's gloss 'circle' is the primary Latin meaning, correctly given.

nodes.derivation: Watkins gives the three together: 'Greek krikos ... (> Latin circus, ring, circle): CIRCA, CIRCLE, CIRCUM-, SEARCH'. circus is the Latin noun taken over unchanged — in English from the late fourteenth century of the Roman arena, and from 1791 of Astley's Royal Circus in London, whence the modern travelling show; circle is Middle English cercle from Old French cercle from Latin circulus, the diminutive of circus (so it reaches English through French, not directly); search is the least obvious member and the best attested — Middle English serchen from Old French cerchier (modern chercher) from Late Latin circāre 'to go round (hence, to explore)', a denominative of circus. Skeat says the same in one line: 'search, to explore. (F. - L.) M.E. serchen, cerchen. - O.F. cerchier. - L. circāre, to go round; hence, to explore. - L. circus, a ring.'

nodes.derivation: All three Germanic stems are genuinely in Pokorny's entry, but they belong to three different extensions and one gloss is wrong. (a) *skrink- : IEW 936, nasalized (s)kreng-, 'Old English scrincan "shrink up, verschrumpfen, wither", Middle Low German schrinken'; Watkins writes it 'Germanic *skrink-'. 'To shrivel up' is a fair gloss. (b) *hringaz : IEW 936, (s)kregh-/(s)krengh-, 'urgerm. *hrengaz in Finnish rengas [a loan], Old Icelandic hringr, Old English, Old Saxon, Old High German hring "ring"'; Wiktionary reconstructs *hringaz 'ring, circle' < PIE *(s)krengʰ-. The gloss 'circle' is acceptable. (c) *hrugjaz : IEW 937-938 puts Old Icelandic hryggr 'backbone, spine', Old English hrycg, Old Saxon hruggi, Old High German (h)rukki 'back' under the k-extension (s)kreu-k-, and Watkins under '*kreuk- in Germanic *hrugjaz'. nodes.derivation: Eight of the nine English words are in Watkins under sker-3, in exactly Nourai's groupings: 'Germanic *skrink- in Old English scrincan ...: SHRINK'; '*hringaz ... a. Old English hring, a ring: RING; b. Old French renc, reng, line, row: RANCH, RANGE, RANK, RINK; ARRANGE, DERANGE'; '*hrugjaz ... Old English hrycg, spine, ridge: RIDGE'. The Romance group goes back to Frankish *hring 'circle (of men drawn up)', borrowed into Gallo-Romance as renc/ranc 'row, rank', whence Old French rangier/arengier > arrange, desrengier > derange, and Spanish rancho 'group messing together' > ranch; rink is the Scots form of the same Old French renc. ribbon is the one item Watkins does not list, and Etymonline calls it 'a word of unknown origin, possibly from a Germanic compound whose second element is related to band; compare Middle Dutch ringhband "necklace"'. Klein states the same derivation positively — 'ribbon, also riband, n. — ME. riban(d), fr. OF. riban, var. of ruban (F. ruban), fr. MDu. ringh-band, "necklace". The first element of this compound is rel. to E. ring' — and that is presumably Nourai's warrant. So ribbon belongs here only on Klein's (possible but unproved) etymology; everything else is confirmed.
